core1b.fresh_task: A beam travels through clear air containing tiny particles; viewed from the side it looks blue while transmitted light is warmer. Explain both observations.
core1b.protected_work: Explain directional color observations using scattering rather than prism dispersion.

stages.attempt: A beam travels through clear air containing tiny particles; viewed from the side it looks blue while transmitted light is warmer. Explain both observations.
stages.reconstruct: Short wavelengths scatter more strongly in Rayleigh regime into side directions, depleting them from transmitted beam; direct spectrum shifts toward longer wavelengths.
stages.diagnose: Only if your saved answer demonstrates this error: Assuming every scattering medium produces blue light. Otherwise record insufficient evidence; compare your actual reasoning with the reconstruction.
stages.repair: Compare particle size with wavelength and distinguish side-scattered from transmitted light.
stages.boundary_test: What if the incident light is monochromatic red?

core1b.fresh_task: Why can a thick cloud look white even though a clear sky looks blue?

stages.attempt: Why can a thick cloud look white even though a clear sky looks blue?
stages.reconstruct: Cloud droplets are much larger than molecules; scattering is less strongly wavelength-selective across visible wavelengths and multiple scattering occurs. All colors together often appear white.
stages.diagnose: Only if your saved answer demonstrates this error: Assuming every scattering medium produces blue light. Otherwise record insufficient evidence; compare your actual reasoning with the reconstruction.

core1b.fresh_task: Two chambers contain tiny molecules and large water droplets. Under white illumination, which supports 1/λ⁴ approximation and why?
core1b.protected_work: Select between Rayleigh approximation, large-particle scattering and refraction from observations.

stages.predict: State your expected result, direction or relationship before solving. Record uncertainty if needed.
stages.attempt: Two chambers contain tiny molecules and large water droplets. Under white illumination, which supports 1/λ⁴ approximation and why?
stages.reconstruct: Molecules much smaller than λ support Rayleigh approximation; large droplets do not. Their scattering requires other treatment.
stages.diagnose: Only if your saved answer demonstrates this error: Using the Rayleigh law for any particles or attributing every color to refraction. Otherwise record insufficient evidence; compare your actual reasoning with the reconstruction.
stages.repair: Identify mechanism and particle-size regime before applying a wavelength law.
stages.boundary_test: How could varying particle size change the wavelength dependence?

core1b.fresh_task: Under ideal Rayleigh assumptions compare scattering at 400 and 600 nm; justify whether ratio alone predicts perceived sky color.
core1b.protected_work: Quantify a conditional scattering ratio and distinguish model limits from observed color.

stages.predict: State your expected result, direction or relationship before solving. Record uncertainty if needed.
stages.attempt: Under ideal Rayleigh assumptions compare scattering at 400 and 600 nm; justify whether ratio alone predicts perceived sky color.
stages.reconstruct: I400/I600=(600/400)^4=5.0625. Perceived color also depends on spectrum, visual sensitivity, path and other effects, so ratio alone insufficient.
stages.diagnose: Only if your saved answer demonstrates this error: Treating wavelength ratio as intensity ratio or as universal color prediction. Otherwise record insufficient evidence; compare your actual reasoning with the reconstruction.
stages.repair: Use fourth-power ratio only in appropriate regime, then state observational limits.
stages.boundary_test: At equal wavelength, what other factors could change scattered intensity?
